disclaimer: Anatomical facts (origin/insertion/action/innervation) are textbook-consensus, sourced and cross-checked against a second independent source. Not medical advice.

structures.name: Rectus femoris
structures.plainName: the straight middle quad on the front of your thigh — the only one of the four that also crosses the hip

origin.text: Two heads: a straight head from the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS), and a reflected head from the bony groove just above the rim of the hip socket (supra-acetabular groove of the ilium).
origin.attachTo: ilium (anterior inferior iliac spine and supra-acetabular groove)

insertion.text: The two heads converge into the quadriceps tendon, which attaches to the base of the patella (kneecap); force is transmitted onward through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
insertion.attachTo: base of the patella, via the quadriceps tendon (continuing as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity)

actions: knee extension (straightening the knee)
hip flexion (lifting the thigh forward)
structures.locate: Sit on a chair, let one leg hang, then straighten your knee and lift your thigh a little off the seat. Feel the long muscle running straight down the centre-front of your thigh — from the front of your hip bone down to your kneecap. It is the ridge that stands up in the middle as you kick your leg out.
structures.palpation: With the patient seated, palpate the central anterior thigh along a line from the anterior inferior iliac spine to the patella while the patient extends the knee and flexes the hip against resistance; the contracting muscle belly rises up under the fingers.
commonProblems: rectus-femoris-strain
anterior-knee-pain
hip-flexor-tightness

structures.name: Vastus medialis
structures.plainName: inner-thigh quad (the teardrop bulge just above and inside your kneecap)
aka: Vastus medialis oblique (VMO, its lower oblique fibres)

origin.text: Along a continuous line on the femur: the lower part of the intertrochanteric line, the spiral line, the medial lip of the linea aspera, and the upper medial supracondylar line, plus the medial intermuscular septum.

insertion.text: Into the medial part of the quadriceps (quadriceps femoris) tendon and the medial border of the patella; via the patella and patellar ligament this pulls on the tibial tuberosity.

actions: knee extension (straightens the knee, with the other quadriceps)
medial patellar stabilisation (its oblique lower fibres, the VMO, help keep the kneecap tracking centrally and stop it drifting laterally)
commonProblems: patellofemoral-pain
patellar-maltracking
vmo-weakness-after-knee-injury
structures.locate: Sit down and straighten one leg hard so the thigh tightens: the soft teardrop-shaped bulge that pops up just above your kneecap and toward the inner side of your leg is the vastus medialis. Press it while you tense and relax the leg and you will feel it firm up and soften.
structures.palpation: With the patient seated and the knee actively extended against gentle resistance, palpate the bulk of muscle immediately superomedial to the patella, feeling it contract as the leg straightens.

structures.name: Vastus lateralis
structures.plainName: outer-thigh quad (the big muscle on the outside of your thigh)

origin.text: Greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line, and the lateral lip of the linea aspera of the femur

insertion.text: Base and lateral border of the patella via the quadriceps tendon, continuing to the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament

actions: knee extension
lateral patellar stabilisation
structures.locate: Sit down and straighten your knee against light resistance, then feel the large muscle bulge on the outer (little-toe) side of your thigh, a hand's width above and to the outside of your kneecap.
structures.palpation: With the knee actively extended, palpate the muscle belly on the anterolateral thigh, roughly 10-15 cm above the superolateral border of the patella, feeling it firm up during quadriceps contraction.
commonProblems: patellofemoral-pain
iliotibial-band-syndrome
lateral-patellar-tracking

structures.name: Vastus intermedius
structures.plainName: the deep middle quad — the part of the front-thigh muscle that lies underneath, buried between the inner and outer quads

origin.text: Upper two-thirds of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the shaft of the femur (thigh bone), plus the lower part of the lateral intermuscular septum

insertion.text: Deep part of the quadriceps tendon, which attaches to the base of the patella (kneecap) and continues via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity

actions: knee extension (straightening the knee)
structures.locate: Because it sits deep, you cannot touch it directly. Sit down and slowly straighten your knee against light resistance: the firm bulk you feel in the middle-front of your thigh, deep beneath the surface muscles, is the vastus intermedius working.
structures.palpation: It is not directly palpable as it lies deep to the rectus femoris; a clinician assesses it indirectly by palpating the anterior thigh for tone/bulk during resisted knee extension.
commonProblems: quadriceps-strain
quadriceps-atrophy
knee-extensor-weakness

structures.name: Biceps femoris
structures.plainName: the outer hamstring (the lateral of the two big muscles at the back of your thigh)

origin.text: Long head: the inferomedial impression of the ischial tuberosity (the sitting bone) and the sacrotuberous ligament. Short head: the lateral lip of the linea aspera and the lateral supracondylar line on the back of the femur (thigh bone).
origin.attachTo: ischial tuberosity (long head) and femur / linea aspera (short head)

insertion.text: The two heads join into a common tendon that attaches mainly to the head of the fibula (the small outer bone of the lower leg, just below and outside the knee), with a slip to the lateral condyle of the tibia.

actions: knee flexion
lateral (external) rotation of the flexed knee
hip extension (long head only)
lateral (external) rotation of the thigh at the hip (long head)
pelvic stabilisation during trunk flexion and gait

innervation.nerve: Long head: tibial division of the sciatic nerve; Short head: common fibular (peroneal) division of the sciatic nerve

structures.locate: Sit with your knee bent and press your fingers into the back of your thigh toward the outer side; trace the firm tendon down to just below and outside the knee, on the outer bony bump of the lower leg (the fibular head). Bending the knee against resistance makes that outer tendon stand out.
structures.palpation: With the patient prone and the knee flexed against resistance, palpate the prominent tendon on the posterolateral aspect of the knee as it runs to the head of the fibula, and follow the muscle belly up the lateral posterior thigh.
commonProblems: hamstring-strain
sciatica-referred-pain
posterolateral-knee-pain

structures.name: Semitendinosus
structures.plainName: one of the three hamstring muscles at the back of the thigh — the long inner-back one whose cord-like tendon you can feel behind the inner side of your knee

origin.text: Lower, medial part of the ischial tuberosity (the sitting bone), by a tendon shared with the long head of biceps femoris

insertion.text: Upper medial surface of the tibia (shinbone), just below the medial condyle, via the pes anserinus — where its tendon blends with those of gracilis and sartorius

actions: knee flexion
hip extension
medial (internal) rotation of the leg at the flexed knee
medial rotation of the thigh at the hip
pelvic stabilisation

innervation.nerve: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve

structures.locate: Sit on a chair, plant your heel, and bend your knee as if dragging the heel back under you — then feel just behind and to the inner (big-toe) side of the back of your knee. The prominent round cord that pops up there is the semitendinosus tendon; trace it upward into the back of your thigh toward your sitting bone.
structures.palpation: With the patient prone and the knee actively flexed against resistance, palpate the medial hamstring tendons at the back of the knee: the semitendinosus is the more superficial, rounded, cord-like tendon lying just lateral (superficial) to the flatter, deeper semimembranosus.
commonProblems: hamstring-strain
proximal-hamstring-tendinopathy
acl-graft-harvest-morbidity

structures.name: Semimembranosus
structures.plainName: inner hamstring (deep muscle on the back-inner side of your thigh)

origin.text: Superolateral impression of the ischial tuberosity (the 'sit bone' at the base of the pelvis), attaching more superiorly than semitendinosus and biceps femoris

insertion.text: Medial condyle of the tibia (the inner side of the top of the shin bone), with additional slips to the medial tibial margin, the lateral condyle of the femur (oblique popliteal ligament) and the fascia over the popliteus muscle

actions: hip extension
knee flexion
internal (medial) rotation of the flexed knee
internal rotation of the hip
pelvic stabilisation

innervation.nerve: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve

structures.locate: Sit down and press your fingers into the back of your thigh just above the crease behind your knee, toward the inner (big-toe) side. Bend your knee against light resistance and you will feel a firm cord-like tendon pop up on that inner side — that is the semimembranosus. It sits deeper and slightly inward compared with the more rope-like semitendinosus tendon next to it.
structures.palpation: Palpate along the posteromedial thigh and over the tendon's insertion on the medial tibial condyle while the patient flexes and internally rotates the knee; tenderness there is typical of semimembranosus tendinopathy.
commonProblems: hamstring-strain
semimembranosus-tendinopathy
posteromedial-knee-pain

structures.name: Gluteus maximus
structures.plainName: the main buttock muscle (the big muscle you sit on)

origin.text: Gluteal (posterior) surface of the ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the posterior surface of the sacrum and coccyx, the thoracolumbar (lumbar) fascia, and the sacrotuberous ligament

insertion.text: The superficial three-quarters form a tendinous sheet inserting into the iliotibial tract of the fascia lata; the deeper fibres insert into the gluteal tuberosity of the femur

actions: hip extension
hip external (lateral) rotation
upper fibres assist hip abduction, lower fibres assist hip adduction
stabilises the extended knee via the iliotibial tract
chief antigravity muscle when rising from sitting
structures.locate: Sit down, then place a hand on the fleshy part of your backside and stand up or squeeze your buttocks together — the large muscle you feel firming up and bulging under your hand is the gluteus maximus.
structures.palpation: With the patient prone, palpate the broad muscle mass of the buttock and feel it contract as they extend the hip against resistance or squeeze the buttocks together.
commonProblems: gluteal-amnesia-underactivity
hip-extension-weakness
low-back-pain

structures.name: Gluteus medius
structures.plainName: side-hip muscle (the fan-shaped muscle on the upper-outer side of your buttock)

origin.text: Outer (gluteal) surface of the ilium, between the iliac crest above and the anterior/posterior gluteal lines, plus the overlying gluteal aponeurosis; lies partly under gluteus maximus.

insertion.text: Oblique ridge on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter of the femur.

actions: hip abduction
stabilisation of the pelvis on the stance leg during single-leg support (walking)
medial/internal rotation and flexion of the hip (anterior fibres)
extension and lateral/external rotation of the hip (posterior fibres)
structures.locate: Put your hand on the upper-outer side of one buttock, roughly a hand's width below the top of your hip bone, then lift that same-side leg out to the side; you'll feel the muscle firm up under your palm.
structures.palpation: Palpated on the lateral hip midway between the iliac crest and the greater trochanter; it firms under the fingers when the patient abducts the hip against resistance or stands on one leg.
commonProblems: gluteal-tendinopathy
trendelenburg-gait
greater-trochanteric-pain-syndrome
hip-abductor-weakness

structures.name: Gluteus minimus
structures.plainName: deepest, smallest buttock muscle (sits under the gluteus medius on the side of your hip)

origin.text: Gluteal (outer) surface of the ilium, between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines, lying deep to the gluteus medius

insertion.text: Anterolateral (front-outer) border of the greater trochanter of the femur, via a converging tendon with an intervening bursa

actions: hip abduction (moving the thigh out to the side)
medial (internal) rotation of the thigh, chiefly by the anterior fibres
stabilisation of the pelvis over the stance leg during walking (prevents the opposite hip dropping)
antagonists: lateral rotator group (e.g. piriformis, obturator internus)
structures.locate: Place your fingertips on the bony point at the very top of your hip bone (iliac crest), then slide down and slightly forward toward the side of your hip; it lies deep beneath the gluteus medius, so you feel it working — not the muscle itself — when you stand on one leg and lift the other foot slightly off the floor, keeping your pelvis level.
structures.palpation: Palpated indirectly on the lateral hip, just below the iliac crest and above the greater trochanter, deep to the gluteus medius, with the patient in side-lying while they actively abduct and internally rotate the thigh.
commonProblems: gluteal-tendinopathy
greater-trochanteric-pain-syndrome
trendelenburg-gait

structures.name: Gastrocnemius
structures.plainName: calf muscle (the two-headed bulge on the back of your lower leg)

origin.text: Two heads from the femur just above the knee: the medial head from the popliteal surface and posterior surface of the medial condyle, and the lateral head from a facet on the upper posterolateral surface of the lateral condyle.

insertion.text: Via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon into the mid-posterior surface of the calcaneus (heel bone).

actions: plantar flexion of the foot at the ankle (pointing the toes down)
flexion of the knee (bending the leg)
structures.locate: Sit and point your toes down hard, or rise up onto the balls of your feet — feel the two firm bumps that bulge out on the back of your lower leg, between the back of your knee and your heel.
structures.palpation: With the patient prone or standing on tiptoe, palpate the two prominent muscle bellies on the superficial posterior calf and follow them distally as they converge into the Achilles tendon above the heel.
commonProblems: calf-strain
achilles-tendinopathy
muscle-cramps

structures.name: Soleus
structures.plainName: the deep calf muscle (the flat one underneath the bulging calf muscle)

origin.text: Posterior surface of the head and upper shaft of the fibula, the soleal line and medial border of the tibia, and a tendinous arch spanning between the two bones

insertion.text: Posterior surface of the calcaneus (heel bone) via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon

actions: plantar flexion of the ankle (pointing the foot/toes downward)
postural stabilisation of the ankle when standing (resisting forward sway of the body)
structures.palpation: With the patient prone and the knee flexed to about 90 degrees (which slackens the gastrocnemius), ask them to plantarflex against resistance and palpate the muscle belly on the medial and lateral sides of the calf, just deep and inferior to the gastrocnemius bulge.
structures.locate: Sit down and bend your knee so your foot is flat on the floor, then push the ball of your foot down against the floor. Feel along the sides of your lower calf, below the rounded bulge of the main calf muscle: the firm band you feel tighten there, closer to the shin bone and deeper down toward the heel, is the soleus. Because your knee is bent, the big surface calf muscle stays slack, so most of what tightens is soleus.
commonProblems: achilles-tendinopathy
calf-strain
chronic-exertional-compartment-syndrome
plantar-flexion-weakness

structures.name: Tibialis anterior
structures.plainName: shin muscle (the strap of muscle running down the front-outer side of your shin)

origin.text: Lateral condyle and upper half-to-two-thirds of the lateral (outer) surface of the tibia, plus the adjacent anterior surface of the interosseous membrane

insertion.text: Medial cuneiform bone and the base of the first metatarsal, on the inner side of the foot's arch

actions: dorsiflexion of the foot at the ankle (talocrural joint)
inversion of the foot at the subtalar joint
structures.locate: Sit down and pull your toes and foot up toward your shin; feel the firm cord of muscle that bulges just to the outer side of your shin bone (tibia), a couple of inches below the knee and running down toward the inner ankle.
structures.palpation: With the ankle in dorsiflexion and inversion, palpate the fleshy muscle belly immediately lateral to the tibial crest in the upper leg, and follow its tendon as it stands out crossing the front of the ankle toward the medial cuneiform.
commonProblems: shin-splints
anterior-compartment-syndrome
foot-drop

structures.name: Multifidus muscle
structures.plainName: Multifidus (deep spine-stabilizer muscles)
structures.locate: Reach behind your lower back and feel the two firm ridges of muscle running vertically just to either side of the bony bumps of your spine. The multifidus sits underneath the more superficial muscles there, right against the spine — you can feel it tighten if you gently arch your lower back or lean slightly to one side while pressing your fingertips into that groove beside the spine.

origin.text: Sacrum and sacroiliac ligament, posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) and iliac crest, common tendinous origin of the erector spinae (erector spinae aponeurosis), mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae, transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae, and articular processes of the lower cervical vertebrae (C4-C7)
origin.attachTo: sacrum, posterior superior iliac spine, and the mammillary/transverse/articular processes of the vertebrae

insertion.text: Spinous processes of the vertebrae above the origin; each fascicle ascends and spans roughly 2 to 4 vertebral segments (some sources describe fascicles reaching up to about five segments)
insertion.attachTo: spinous processes of the vertebrae above (roughly 2-4 levels superior)

actions: Bilateral contraction extends the vertebral column (backward bending)
Unilateral contraction produces ipsilateral lateral flexion (side-bending toward the same side)
Unilateral contraction produces contralateral rotation (rotating the spine toward the opposite side)
Stabilizes the individual vertebrae and vertebral joints, acting like an adjustable ligament
Provides proprioceptive feedback owing to its high muscle-spindle density

innervation.nerve: Medial branches of the posterior (dorsal) rami of the spinal nerves
innervation.roots: Segmental, at the corresponding vertebral levels

commonProblems: Atrophy and fatty infiltration strongly associated with chronic and recurrent low back pain
Reflex inhibition and delayed reactivation after an episode of back pain, contributing to high recurrence rates
Impaired segmental spinal stability when deconditioned
structures.palpation: Palpated in the paraspinal groove immediately lateral to the spinous processes, deep to the erector spinae; most accessible in the lumbar region with the subject prone.

structures.name: Rectus abdominis muscle
structures.plainName: Abs (the "six-pack" muscle)

origin.text: Pubic crest and pubic symphysis (bony ridge at the front base of the pelvis, just above the genitals)

insertion.text: Xiphoid process of the sternum and costal cartilages of the 5th, 6th and 7th ribs (the lower front of the breastbone and rib margin)

actions: Flexes the trunk / lumbar spine (bends the torso forward, as in a sit-up or crunch)
Compresses the abdominal contents and raises intra-abdominal pressure (assists forced exhalation, coughing, defecation, childbirth)
Stabilizes and controls tilt of the pelvis (antilordosis)

innervation.nerve: Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7-T11) and the subcostal nerve (T12)

structures.locate: Sit or lie down and lift your head and shoulders off the surface as if starting a sit-up. Press your fingertips into the front of your belly, in the vertical strip running from just below your breastbone down to your pubic bone, a couple of centimetres to either side of your navel. The firm band that tightens under your fingers is the rectus abdominis.
structures.palpation: With the person lying on their back, ask them to raise their head and shoulders (a partial curl-up). Palpate the tensed vertical band on either side of the midline (linea alba) between the pubic bone and the xiphoid/lower ribs. The horizontal tendinous intersections create the segmented "six-pack" feel in lean individuals.
commonProblems: Diastasis recti (separation of the two muscle bellies along the midline, common after pregnancy)
Abdominal muscle strain from overuse or sudden loading
Rectus sheath hematoma (bleeding within the muscle sheath)

structures.name: Quadratus lumborum muscle
structures.plainName: Quadratus lumborum (deep side muscle of the lower back)

origin.text: Posterior part of the iliac crest and the iliolumbar ligament
origin.attachTo: iliac crest (back rim of the pelvis) and iliolumbar ligament

insertion.text: Inferior (lower) border of the 12th rib and the transverse processes of the L1-L4 lumbar vertebrae
insertion.attachTo: lower border of the 12th rib and the transverse processes of lumbar vertebrae L1-L4

actions: Unilateral (one side): lateral flexion of the trunk toward the same side
Bilateral (both sides together): extension of the lumbar spine and trunk stabilization
Fixes (anchors) the 12th rib during inspiration, acting as an accessory muscle of respiration
Stabilizes the lumbar spine and pelvis, and helps elevate (hitch) the hip

innervation.nerve: Subcostal nerve and anterior rami of the upper lumbar spinal nerves

structures.locate: Put your hands on your waist with thumbs pointing back. Slide your thumbs inward and down toward the soft area between the bottom of your ribcage and the top of your hip bone, just to the side of your spine. Press gently in and lean slightly to that side to feel it tighten. This is the deep muscle that aches when your lower back feels sore on one side after standing too long.
structures.palpation: With the person lying on their side or standing, find the gap between the lowest rib (12th rib) and the top of the pelvis (iliac crest), a couple of finger-widths to the side of the spine. Press firmly and deeply into this soft space; the muscle lies deep to the erector spinae. Side-bending toward the same side makes it contract under your fingers.
antagonists: Quadratus lumborum of the opposite side
commonProblems: Low back pain and stiffness, often one-sided, from prolonged sitting or standing
Muscle spasm or trigger points referring pain to the hip and buttock region
Tightness and pelvic imbalance associated with a leg-length difference or habitual hip-hiking
Fatigue-related aching after activities involving repeated bending or lifting

structures.name: Transversus abdominis
structures.plainName: Deep abdominal corset muscle

origin.text: Internal surfaces of the costal cartilages of ribs 7-12, the thoracolumbar fascia, the anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest, and the lateral third of the inguinal ligament
origin.attachTo: Costal cartilages 7-12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, inguinal ligament

insertion.text: Linea alba (via its aponeurosis, extending from the xiphoid process to the pubis), the pubic crest and pecten pubis; the lower fibres join the internal oblique aponeurosis to form the conjoint tendon
insertion.attachTo: Linea alba (xiphoid process to pubis), pubic crest, pecten pubis (via conjoint tendon)

actions: Compresses the abdominal contents and increases intra-abdominal pressure (bilateral contraction)
Assists forced expiration
Supports the abdominal viscera and stabilises the lumbar spine and pelvis
May weakly assist ipsilateral trunk rotation (unilateral contraction); rotation is minor and disputed given the largely transverse fibre orientation

innervation.nerve: Thoracoabdominal (lower intercostal) nerves, subcostal nerve, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves

structures.locate: Place your fingertips about 2-3 cm inward from the front of your hip bone, then gently cough or draw your belly button toward your spine without holding your breath. The deep, even tightening you feel band around your waist beneath the more superficial muscles is the transversus abdominis wrapping like a corset.
structures.palpation: Lie on your back with knees bent. Rest your fingers just inward from the front of the pelvic bone (anterior superior iliac spine). Perform a gentle 'draw-in' by flattening your lower belly without bulging or bracing hard; you should feel a light, deep tension develop under your fingers rather than the bulk of the obliques.
commonProblems: Delayed or weak activation is associated with lumbopelvic and low-back pain
Coordination loss after pregnancy, often alongside diastasis recti (separation of the linea alba)
Substitution by bracing or bulging the outer abdominals instead of performing the deep draw-in

structures.name: Erector spinae
structures.plainName: the paired muscle columns running up either side of your spine that straighten and support your back

origin.text: A broad common tendon attaching to the medial crest of the sacrum, the medial part of the iliac crest, the spinous processes of the lumbar and lower thoracic vertebrae, and the supraspinous ligament
origin.attachTo: sacrum, iliac crest, and lumbar/lower-thoracic spinous processes

insertion.text: The three columns run upward and insert onto the angles of the ribs and the transverse and spinous processes of the thoracic and cervical vertebrae, with the highest slips (longissimus capitis, spinalis capitis) reaching the mastoid process and occipital bone of the skull
insertion.attachTo: ribs, thoracic/cervical vertebrae, and base of the skull

actions: Bilaterally extends (straightens/arches) the vertebral column
Unilaterally laterally flexes the vertebral column to the same side
Controls forward bending of the trunk by eccentric contraction and stabilises posture in standing and sitting
Upper (capitis) slips help extend and rotate the head

innervation.roots: Lateral branches of the posterior rami of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal nerves

structures.locate: Reach behind you and press your fingertips a couple of centimetres either side of the bony ridge of your lower spine; you will feel two firm, rope-like vertical columns of muscle. Arch backwards or lift your chest and they tighten under your fingers.
structures.palpation: Sit or stand and place your fingers just lateral to the spinous processes in the lower back. Extend (arch) the trunk backward against gravity and you feel the paired muscular ridges bulge and firm up on either side of the midline.
commonProblems: Low back muscle strain from lifting or sudden twisting
Chronic tension and spasm from prolonged sitting or poor posture
Overuse soreness after heavy deadlifting or repeated bending

structures.name: Abdominal external oblique muscle
structures.plainName: Side abs (the outer "love-handle" muscles)

origin.text: External surface of the lower eight ribs (ribs 5-12), interdigitating with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi

insertion.text: Via a broad aponeurosis into the linea alba, pubic tubercle, and the anterior half of the iliac crest (fleshy fibres attach directly to the iliac crest)
insertion.attachTo: linea alba, iliac crest, pubic tubercle

actions: Flexion of the trunk (both sides contracting together)
Contralateral rotation of the trunk (turning the torso to the opposite side)
Lateral flexion of the trunk to the same side (one side contracting)
Compression of the abdominal contents, raising intra-abdominal pressure

innervation.nerve: Thoracoabdominal nerves (lower intercostal nerves) and subcostal nerve

structures.locate: Place a flat hand on the side of your waist, just below your ribs and above your hip bone. Cough or twist your upper body toward the opposite side and you will feel this muscle tighten under your fingers along your side and lower ribs.
structures.palpation: Sit or stand and lay your fingers on the fleshy area between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone, at the side-front of your waist. Rotate your torso to the opposite side or brace as if about to be poked in the stomach; the muscle firms up under your fingertips.
commonProblems: Abdominal muscle strain ("side ab" pull) from twisting or forceful rotation
Contributes to the wall of inguinal hernias via its aponeurosis and the inguinal ligament

structures.name: Latissimus dorsi muscle
structures.plainName: Lats (the broad muscle across your mid and lower back)

origin.text: Spinous processes of the T7–T12 vertebrae, the thoracolumbar fascia, the posterior iliac crest, the lower 3–4 ribs, and often the inferior angle of the scapula
origin.attachTo: Lower thoracic and lumbar spine, iliac crest, lower ribs, and inferior angle of the scapula

insertion.text: Floor of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus, between the pectoralis major and teres major insertions

actions: Extends the flexed arm (pulls the raised arm down and back)
Adducts the arm (brings the arm toward the body)
Internally (medially) rotates the arm
Assists in drawing the shoulder girdle downward and backward when the arm is fixed
Assists forced expiration and deep breathing

innervation.nerve: Thoracodorsal nerve (a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus)

structures.locate: Reach across with the opposite hand to just below and behind your armpit, on the side of your back. Push your elbow down and inward against your ribs as if starting a pull-up, and you will feel a broad sheet of muscle firm up and fan out toward your lower back.
structures.palpation: Sit or stand with your arm slightly away from your body. Place your fingers on the fleshy fold that forms the back wall of your armpit (posterior axillary fold). Push your elbow down and back, or cough forcefully; the latissimus tenses under your fingers and can be traced downward toward the lower ribs and pelvis.
commonProblems: Tightness limiting overhead reach, often felt when raising the arms fully overhead
Contributes to rounded-shoulder and forward-shoulder posture when short and tight
Trigger points that refer aching pain to the mid-back, under the shoulder blade, and down the inner arm
Strain or tears from heavy pulling, rowing, or swimming

structures.name: Levator scapulae muscle
structures.plainName: Shoulder-blade lifter (the muscle running from the side of your neck to the top corner of your shoulder blade)

origin.text: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the upper four cervical vertebrae (C1-C4)

insertion.text: Superior (upper) part of the medial border of the scapula, between the superior angle and the root of the spine of the scapula
insertion.attachTo: superior angle and upper medial border of the scapula

actions: Elevates the scapula (lifts the shoulder blade upward)
Rotates the scapula so the glenoid cavity tilts downward (downward rotation)
When the scapula is fixed, laterally flexes the neck to the same side (ipsilateral)
Assists in extension of the neck

innervation.nerve: Dorsal scapular nerve, with additional supply from the anterior rami of cervical spinal nerves C3 and C4
innervation.roots: C3, C4, and C5 (dorsal scapular nerve)

structures.locate: Reach across the back of your neck to the top inner corner of your shoulder blade (a few centimetres out from your spine, level with the base of your neck). The levator scapulae runs upward and forward from that corner to the side of your neck, tucked deep to the fleshy upper trapezius. Shrug your shoulder up toward your ear and you feel this region tense — it is the muscle that does the lifting.
structures.palpation: Sits deep to the upper trapezius. To feel it, tilt your head slightly toward the same side to relax the trapezius, then press your fingers just above the superior angle of the shoulder blade (the top inner corner) while gently shrugging; the taut cord you feel angling up toward the neck is the levator scapulae.
commonProblems: A frequent site of neck-and-shoulder tension and trigger points, especially from prolonged desk/screen posture or carrying bags on one shoulder
Tightness can restrict turning the head and produce a stiff, aching neck at the base of the skull-to-shoulder line

structures.name: Trapezius muscle
structures.plainName: Trapezius (the large diamond-shaped muscle across the back of your neck and upper back)
structures.locate: Reach one hand over the opposite shoulder to the fleshy ridge between your neck and the point of your shoulder, then shrug that shoulder up toward your ear — the band that tightens and lifts under your fingers is the upper trapezius. It fans down as a large flat sheet covering the back of the neck and the upper back, running from the base of the skull down the spine to the middle of the back.
structures.palpation: Sit tall and let your arms hang. Pinch the soft ridge of muscle on top of the shoulder halfway between neck and shoulder tip, then shrug — you will feel it firm up. To feel the lower part, place a hand between your shoulder blade and spine and pull the shoulder blade down and back.

origin.text: Medial third of the superior nuchal line and external occipital protuberance of the skull, the nuchal ligament, and the spinous processes of the C7 to T12 vertebrae
origin.attachTo: Superior nuchal line and external occipital protuberance of the occipital bone, nuchal ligament, and spinous processes of vertebrae C7-T12

insertion.text: Posterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion, and the spine of the scapula
insertion.attachTo: Lateral third of the clavicle, acromion process, and spine of the scapula

actions: Elevates the scapula (shrugging the shoulder, via upper fibers)
Retracts the scapula, drawing it toward the spine (via middle fibers)
Depresses the scapula (via lower fibers)
Upwardly rotates the scapula so the arm can be raised overhead (upper and lower fibers acting together)
Extends and laterally flexes the head and neck (upper fibers, when the scapula is fixed)

innervation.nerve: Accessory nerve (CN XI) provides the motor supply; the anterior rami of cervical spinal nerves C3 and C4 supply proprioceptive fibers (some sources also describe an additional motor contribution)

synergists: Serratus anterior (in upward rotation of the scapula)
commonProblems: Upper-trapezius tension and trigger points from prolonged desk or screen posture, often felt as neck-and-shoulder tightness or tension headaches
Weakness or poor control of the middle and lower fibers contributing to rounded-shoulder posture and shoulder-blade instability
Strain from carrying heavy bags on one shoulder

structures.name: Rhomboid major muscle
structures.plainName: Rhomboid major (the shoulder-blade squeezer between your spine and inner shoulder blade)

origin.text: Spinous processes of the T2 to T5 thoracic vertebrae (and the supraspinous ligament between them)

insertion.text: Medial (vertebral) border of the scapula, between the root of the scapular spine and the inferior angle, just below the insertion of rhomboid minor

actions: Retracts the scapula, drawing the shoulder blade toward the spine
Rotates the scapula downward so the glenoid cavity (shoulder socket) points down
Fixes and stabilises the scapula against the thoracic wall
structures.locate: Sit or stand and reach one arm across the front of your body to the opposite side. With that hand, feel the area between your spine and the inner edge of the other shoulder blade. Now pull both shoulder blades back and down as if pinching a pencil between them — the muscle that firms up in that gap, running diagonally from spine to shoulder-blade edge, is the rhomboid major.
structures.palpation: Ask the person to place the back of their hand on their lower back (hand-behind-back position), which protracts the scapula and makes the rhomboids stand out. Palpate the soft tissue in the triangle between the spine (T2-T5 levels), the medial border of the scapula, and the trapezius above it. Resisted retraction (drawing the shoulder blade toward the spine against resistance) makes it contract and become more prominent.
commonProblems: Weakness or lengthening from prolonged forward-hunched (rounded-shoulder) posture, contributing to scapular protraction
Trigger points causing aching pain between the spine and shoulder blade
Scapular winging or dyskinesis when rhomboid function is impaired

structures.name: Supraspinatus muscle
structures.plainName: Supraspinatus (top rotator-cuff muscle)

origin.text: Medial two-thirds of the supraspinous fossa on the back of the scapula (the shallow groove above the horizontal ridge on the shoulder blade)

insertion.text: Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus, blending with the shoulder joint capsule

actions: Initiates abduction of the arm at the shoulder (first ~15 degrees, before the deltoid takes over)
Assists the deltoid through continued abduction
Stabilizes the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity as part of the rotator cuff
structures.locate: Reach over the top of your opposite shoulder and press into the muscle just above the bony ridge (spine) of the shoulder blade, tucked under the upper trapezius. It sits deep, so you feel it best when you slowly lift that arm sideways a few inches.
structures.palpation: Deep to the trapezius in the supraspinous fossa above the scapular spine; press firmly through the trapezius while the person begins to lift the arm sideways to feel it tense.
commonProblems: Rotator cuff tears (supraspinatus is the most commonly torn cuff tendon)
Subacromial impingement, where the tendon is pinched under the acromion
Tendinopathy or calcific tendinitis causing pain when lifting the arm to shoulder height (painful arc)

structures.name: Subscapularis muscle
structures.plainName: Subscapularis (inner shoulder-blade rotator cuff muscle)

origin.text: Subscapular fossa — the broad concave inner (rib-facing) surface of the shoulder blade — and the tendinous septa along its ridges

insertion.text: Lesser tubercle of the humerus (a small bony bump on the front of the upper arm bone), with fibres blending into the front of the shoulder joint capsule

actions: Internally (medially) rotates the humerus at the shoulder
Adducts the arm (draws it toward the body) to a lesser extent
Stabilizes the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity as part of the rotator cuff

innervation.nerve: Upper and lower subscapular nerves (from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus)

structures.locate: Sit with your elbow tucked at your side and your forearm pointing forward. Rotate that forearm inward across your belly (as if reaching for the opposite hip) — the deep muscle on the front of your shoulder blade, sandwiched between the blade and the rib cage, is the subscapularis doing that work. It sits too deep under the shoulder blade to feel directly by hand.
structures.palpation: Cannot be reliably palpated from the surface — it lies on the front (rib-facing) side of the shoulder blade, roughly 3–5 cm deep beneath the ribs and overlying muscles. Its function is instead assessed indirectly with clinical tests such as the Gerber lift-off test or bear-hug test.
commonProblems: Rotator cuff tears (subscapularis tears cause weak internal rotation and a positive lift-off/bear-hug test)
Subacromial or subcoracoid impingement of the tendon
Tendinopathy contributing to shoulder pain and stiffness

structures.name: Infraspinatus muscle
structures.plainName: Infraspinatus (rear rotator-cuff muscle)

origin.text: Infraspinous fossa of the scapula (the broad hollow on the back of the shoulder blade below its spine)

insertion.text: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus, and the posterior shoulder joint capsule

actions: Externally (laterally) rotates the arm at the shoulder
Stabilizes the glenohumeral joint by pressing the head of the humerus into the socket
Assists in horizontal abduction of the arm
structures.locate: Reach across with your opposite hand to the back of your shoulder blade, just below the bony ridge (the spine of the scapula). Keep your elbow tucked at your side and rotate your forearm outward away from your belly — the muscle you feel firming up over the lower-back part of the shoulder blade is the infraspinatus.
structures.palpation: With the arm relaxed at the side, place fingertips on the flat back surface of the shoulder blade below its horizontal ridge. Resist as you rotate the forearm outward (elbow bent 90 degrees, tucked in) and feel the muscle contract beneath the fingers.
commonProblems: Rotator cuff tears (infraspinatus is a common site)
Tendinopathy causing posterior shoulder pain and weak external rotation
Trigger points referring pain into the front of the shoulder and down the arm
Suprascapular nerve entrapment causing infraspinatus atrophy and weakness

structures.name: Deltoid muscle
structures.plainName: Shoulder muscle (the rounded cap on top of the shoulder)

origin.text: Anterior border and superior surface of the lateral third of the clavicle (clavicular/anterior part), the acromion (acromial/middle part), and the lower lip of the spine of the scapula (spinal/posterior part).
origin.attachTo: lateral third of clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula

insertion.text: Converges to a strong tendon inserting on the deltoid tuberosity, located about halfway down the lateral surface of the shaft of the humerus.

actions: Shoulder (arm) abduction — chiefly the middle/acromial fibers, beyond about 15 degrees
Shoulder flexion and internal rotation — anterior/clavicular fibers
Shoulder extension and external rotation — posterior/spinal fibers
Stabilizes the glenohumeral joint, e.g. when carrying loads
synergists: Pectoralis major (anterior fibers, for flexion/internal rotation)
commonProblems: Deltoid strain from overload or throwing/lifting
Axillary nerve injury (e.g. from shoulder dislocation or surgical neck of humerus fracture) causing deltoid weakness and loss of the rounded shoulder contour
Subacromial/rotator-cuff pain that limits abduction and loads the deltoid
structures.locate: Place your opposite hand over the rounded muscle that caps the very top and outer corner of your shoulder, between your collarbone in front and your shoulder blade behind. Lift your arm straight out to the side and you will feel this muscle bunch up and harden as it does the work.
structures.palpation: With the arm relaxed at the side, feel the soft rounded mass over the top and outer point of the shoulder; ask the person to abduct the arm against gentle resistance and the muscle firms up under your fingers, its three parts (front, side, back) becoming distinct.

structures.name: Serratus anterior muscle
structures.plainName: Boxer's muscle (the finger-like muscle on the side of the ribs, under the armpit)
structures.locate: Reach your hand up under your armpit onto the side of your ribcage. Push your arm forward against a wall as if punching, and you'll feel a set of fan-like muscular fingers tighten along your side ribs, just below the armpit and in front of the lats. In lean people these show as a row of sawtooth ridges over the ribs.
structures.palpation: With the arm raised and pushing forward against resistance, press your fingers onto the outer surface of the ribs just below and forward of the armpit; you can feel the muscular slips contract over ribs 4-8 along the mid-axillary line.

origin.text: Fleshy slips (digitations) from the outer surface of the upper 1st to 8th or 9th ribs

insertion.text: Costal (rib-facing) surface of the medial border of the scapula, from the superior angle to the inferior angle

actions: Protracts the scapula (draws the shoulder blade forward around the ribcage, as in a punch or reaching forward)
Holds the medial border of the scapula against the ribcage, preventing scapular winging
Rotates the scapula upward, allowing the arm to be raised overhead above 90 degrees
Acts as an accessory muscle of inspiration when the shoulder girdle is fixed
commonProblems: Scapular winging - injury to the long thoracic nerve paralyses the muscle, causing the medial border of the shoulder blade to protrude away from the ribcage
Weakness impairs overhead arm elevation and reaching/pushing movements

structures.name: Brachioradialis
structures.plainName: Forearm flexor (thumb-side)

origin.text: Proximal (upper) portion of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus (just above the elbow, on the thumb side of the upper arm bone)

insertion.text: Lateral side of the distal radius, just proximal to the styloid process at the wrist

actions: Flexes the elbow (bends the forearm toward the upper arm)
Strongest as an elbow flexor when the forearm is in a mid/neutral, thumb-up position
Assists in rotating the forearm toward a neutral mid-position (pronating from a supinated position and supinating from a pronated position)
structures.locate: Rest your forearm on a table with your thumb pointing up, then bend your elbow against light resistance (or lift a bottle). The muscle that pops up as a prominent ridge running from just below the outer elbow crease down toward the thumb-side of your wrist is the brachioradialis.
structures.palpation: With the elbow bent about 90 degrees and the thumb pointing up, resist someone pushing your forearm down; the brachioradialis stands out as a firm cord on the upper thumb-side of the forearm, easily grasped between finger and thumb near the elbow.

structures.name: Pectoralis minor
structures.plainName: Small chest muscle (under the pecs)

origin.text: Anterior surface of the 3rd, 4th and 5th ribs, near the costal cartilages, and the fascia over the adjacent intercostal muscles

insertion.text: Medial border and superior surface of the coracoid process of the scapula

actions: Draws the scapula forward and downward (protraction and depression), stabilising it against the chest wall
Rotates the scapula downward (tips the glenoid cavity inferiorly)
Raises the 3rd-5th ribs during forced inspiration when the scapula is fixed (accessory muscle of breathing)

innervation.nerve: Medial pectoral nerve (with a contribution from the lateral pectoral nerve via the ansa pectoralis)

structures.locate: Place your fingertips just below the outer end of your collarbone, near the front of the shoulder, then press inward through the thick pectoralis major. The pectoralis minor is the thin, flat muscle lying underneath, running from your upper front ribs up to the bony hook (coracoid process) at the front tip of your shoulder blade. You can feel it tighten if you push your shoulder forward and down.
structures.palpation: With the pectoralis major relaxed, palpate deep and slightly medial to the coracoid process (the bony bump on the front of the shoulder). Ask the person to reach the hand behind the small of their back and gently push it backward against light resistance; the pectoralis minor contracts and can be felt tensing beneath the pectoralis major in the anterior axillary fold.
commonProblems: Tightness or shortening pulls the scapula into a forward-tilted, protracted position, contributing to rounded-shoulder posture
Can compress the neurovascular bundle beneath it, a cause of (pectoralis minor / neurogenic) thoracic outlet syndrome with arm numbness or tingling
Referred pain over the front of the shoulder and down the inner arm from trigger points

structures.name: Triceps brachii muscle
structures.plainName: Triceps (back of the upper arm)

origin.text: Three heads: the long head from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula (just below the shoulder socket); the lateral head from the posterior humerus above the radial (spiral) groove; the medial head from the posterior humerus below the radial groove.
origin.attachTo: infraglenoid tubercle of scapula; posterior surface of humerus

insertion.text: Common tendon onto the posterior aspect of the olecranon process of the ulna (the point of the elbow).

actions: Extends the forearm at the elbow (straightens the arm)
Long head extends the arm at the shoulder
Long head adducts the arm at the shoulder
Long head helps stabilise the shoulder joint
structures.locate: Rest one arm straight down. With your other hand, feel the fleshy mass on the BACK of your upper arm, opposite the biceps. Straighten your elbow hard (as if pushing something away) and you will feel it firm up. Trace it down to the bony tip of your elbow, where its tendon attaches.
structures.palpation: With the elbow slightly bent, press into the back of the upper arm and ask the person to straighten the elbow against resistance; the three heads bulge and firm under your fingers, and the common tendon can be traced to the point of the elbow.
commonProblems: Triceps tendinopathy or tendon strain from repetitive pushing/pressing loads
Distal triceps tendon rupture (uncommon) causing weak elbow extension
Weak elbow extension after radial nerve injury (e.g. mid-shaft humerus fracture)

structures.name: Adductor longus muscle
structures.plainName: Inner-thigh muscle (adductor longus)

origin.text: Body of the pubis, just below the pubic crest and next to the pubic symphysis (front of the pelvis)

insertion.text: Middle third of the linea aspera, the rough ridge running down the back of the thigh bone (femur)

actions: Adducts the hip (pulls the thigh inward toward the midline)
Flexes the hip (helps lift the thigh forward)
May assist in rotation of the thigh at the hip, though whether it contributes to medial or lateral rotation is debated between sources
Helps stabilise the pelvis during standing and walking

innervation.nerve: Anterior branch of the obturator nerve

structures.locate: Sit down and squeeze your knees together against your own hands. Run your fingers up the inner thigh toward the groin: the firm cord you feel tighten near the top, just below where the leg meets the pelvis, is the adductor longus. It is the most prominent of the inner-thigh muscles you can grab.
structures.palpation: With the hip slightly flexed, abducted and externally rotated, resist adduction; the adductor longus stands out as the most palpable tendon at the medial groin, easily grasped between finger and thumb where it attaches to the pubis.
commonProblems: Groin strain (adductor strain), a common sports injury from sprinting, kicking or sudden changes of direction
Adductor tendinopathy causing chronic groin pain
Overuse pain in field sports, football and hockey

structures.name: Brachialis muscle
structures.plainName: The deep elbow-bending muscle that sits underneath the biceps

origin.text: Anterior surface of the distal half of the humerus (the front of the upper-arm bone, below the deltoid attachment)

insertion.text: Coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna (the front of the ulna just past the elbow joint)

actions: Flexion of the forearm at the elbow joint

innervation.nerve: Musculocutaneous nerve (with a small lateral part supplied by the radial nerve)

structures.locate: Bend your elbow so your forearm comes up toward your shoulder. The big bulge on the front of your upper arm is the biceps; the brachialis lies underneath and just below it, closest to the elbow. To feel it, straighten your arm slightly and press your fingers into the front-outer edge of your lower upper arm, just above the elbow crease and a little toward the thumb side, then bend the elbow against light resistance and feel the firm muscle harden there beside the biceps.
structures.palpation: Palpate on the anterolateral aspect of the lower arm, just lateral to the biceps tendon and proximal to the elbow crease. Ask the person to flex the elbow against resistance with the forearm pronated (palm down) to minimise biceps involvement; the brachialis is felt as a firm band deep and lateral to the biceps, above the elbow joint.
commonProblems: Strain or overuse from repetitive or heavy elbow-flexion loading (e.g. curls, rock climbing, carrying)
Can compress or irritate the musculocutaneous nerve nearby, which may cause forearm sensory changes and weak elbow flexion

structures.name: Gracilis muscle
structures.plainName: Inner-thigh strap muscle

origin.text: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis, extending onto the adjoining ischial ramus (the ischiopubic ramus).

insertion.text: Medial surface of the proximal (upper) shaft of the tibia, via the pes anserinus tendon shared with sartorius and semitendinosus.

actions: Adducts the thigh at the hip (draws the leg inward toward the midline)
Flexes the knee
Medially (internally) rotates the leg at the knee when the knee is bent
Assists weakly with hip flexion

innervation.nerve: Anterior branch of the obturator nerve

structures.locate: Sit down and squeeze your knees together against your own fist placed between them. Run your fingers up the very innermost edge of your thigh, near the surface, from just above the inner knee toward the groin — the long, thin cord-like band you feel tighten there is the gracilis. It is the most superficial of the inner-thigh muscles, so it is the one closest to your skin along that inside seam.
structures.palpation: With the person seated or supine and the hip slightly abducted, resist active adduction; the gracilis stands out as a thin, superficial band along the medial thigh, easiest to trace toward its tendon just above the inner knee (part of the pes anserinus).
commonProblems: Groin (adductor) strain, often felt as a pull along the inner thigh during sudden change-of-direction or kicking movements
Tenderness at the pes anserinus insertion near the inner knee (pes anserine bursitis/tendinopathy)

structures.name: Biceps brachii muscle
structures.plainName: Biceps

origin.text: Two heads on the scapula (shoulder blade): the short head from the coracoid process, and the long head from the supraglenoid tubercle, just above the shoulder socket.

insertion.text: The two heads join into one tendon that attaches to the radial tuberosity of the radius (forearm bone on the thumb side); it also spreads out as the bicipital aponeurosis into the deep fascia on the inner (medial) side of the forearm.

actions: Flexes the elbow (bends the forearm up toward the shoulder)
Supinates the forearm (rotates the palm to face upward), its strongest action, especially with the elbow bent
Weakly flexes the shoulder (raises the arm forward)
structures.locate: Bend your elbow to about a right angle and turn your palm up as if holding a bowl of soup. Look at the front of your upper arm, between shoulder and elbow: the rounded muscle that bulges up is your biceps. This is the classic "make a muscle" bump.
structures.palpation: With your other hand, wrap your fingers around the front of your upper arm midway between shoulder and elbow. Now curl your forearm up (or turn your palm firmly upward against resistance) and you will feel the muscle tighten and harden into a ball under your fingers. Follow it downward toward the crease of your elbow and you can feel its tendon become a firm cord that you can pluck like a guitar string.
commonProblems: Biceps tendinitis: irritation of the long-head tendon at the front of the shoulder, causing aching pain worsened by overhead or lifting activity
Proximal (long head) biceps tendon tear: often causes a bulging 'Popeye' deformity in the mid-upper arm
Distal biceps tendon rupture: a tear at the elbow attachment, usually from a sudden heavy load on a bent arm, weakening supination and elbow flexion
Delayed-onset muscle soreness after curls or other resistance training

structures.name: Tensor fasciae latae muscle
structures.plainName: Tensor fasciae latae (TFL) — the small hip muscle just below your front hip-bone

origin.text: Anterior part of the outer lip of the iliac crest and the outer surface of the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
origin.attachTo: iliac crest (outer lip, front) and anterior superior iliac spine

insertion.text: Iliotibial tract (fascia lata), which continues down to attach at the lateral condyle of the tibia (Gerdy's tubercle); its fascial fibres also blend into the lateral patellar retinaculum
insertion.attachTo: iliotibial tract, continuing to the lateral condyle of the tibia

actions: Abducts the hip (moves the thigh out to the side)
Flexes the hip (lifts the thigh forward)
Medially (internally) rotates the thigh
Tensions the iliotibial tract, helping stabilize the hip and knee during standing and walking
antagonists: Gluteus maximus (opposes hip flexion and medial rotation)
Adductor muscles of the thigh (oppose hip abduction)
synergists: Gluteus maximus (via shared iliotibial tract insertion)
structures.locate: Stand up and place your fingers on the bony bump at the front of your hip (the point where your front pocket meets your waistband). Slide your fingers about two finger-widths down and slightly out onto the soft muscle. Now lift that leg's knee up and slightly out to the side, or turn the foot inward — you should feel a small muscle tighten under your fingers. That firm bulge is the tensor fasciae latae.
structures.palpation: Lie on your back or stand. Find the anterior superior iliac spine (the front hip-bone point), then move about 2 cm down and lateral onto the muscle belly. Actively abduct and internally rotate the hip against light resistance — the TFL will bulge and firm up, making it easy to feel just in front of the gluteus medius.
commonProblems: Tightness or trigger points that contribute to lateral hip and outer-thigh pain
Overactivity linked to iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome and lateral knee pain, common in runners and cyclists
Can contribute to a compensatory hip-hike or gait changes when gluteus medius is weak

structures.name: Pectoralis major muscle
structures.plainName: Big chest muscle
structures.locate: Put your hand flat on the front of your chest, just below the collarbone and above the nipple. Press your palm firmly against a wall or push your two palms together in front of you: the thick fan of muscle that hardens and bulges on either side of your breastbone is the pectoralis major. It stretches from your breastbone across to where your armpit meets the front of your upper arm.
structures.palpation: With one arm, push your palm hard against a wall at chest height. Feel the front of the chest with the other hand: the broad muscle that tightens from the breastbone out toward the armpit fold is the pectoralis major. Its lower border forms the front wall of the armpit and can be pinched between finger and thumb.

origin.text: Clavicular head: anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle (collarbone). Sternocostal head: anterior surface of the sternum (breastbone) and the costal cartilages of the upper six ribs. A small abdominal part arises from the aponeurosis over the upper abdomen (variously described as the aponeurosis of the external oblique or the anterior layer of the rectus sheath).
origin.attachTo: clavicle, sternum, and upper costal cartilages

insertion.text: Both heads converge to a flat tendon that attaches to the lateral lip of the bicipital (intertubercular) groove of the humerus, on the front of the upper arm bone.
insertion.attachTo: lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus

actions: Adducts the arm at the shoulder (draws the upper arm toward the midline of the body)
Medially (internally) rotates the arm at the shoulder
Flexes the arm at the shoulder, chiefly via the clavicular head (lifts the arm forward)
Extends the flexed arm back toward the body, chiefly via the sternocostal head
Horizontal adduction of the arm (as in a bench press or hugging motion)
Assists in drawing the scapula anteriorly and inferiorly

innervation.nerve: Lateral pectoral nerve and medial pectoral nerve (from the brachial plexus)
innervation.roots: C5-T1 overall (clavicular head predominantly C5-C6 via the lateral pectoral nerve; sternocostal head predominantly C7, C8, T1)

commonProblems: Strains or tears of the muscle or its tendon, often from heavy bench pressing
Soreness and tightness after pushing exercises
Rare rupture at the humeral tendon attachment causing bruising and a visible defect in the chest contour

structures.name: Flexor carpi radialis muscle
structures.plainName: Flexor carpi radialis (a forearm muscle that bends the wrist toward the palm and tilts the hand toward the thumb)

origin.text: Medial epicondyle of the humerus, via the common flexor tendon

insertion.text: Bases of the second and third metacarpal bones (palmar surface)

actions: Flexion of the wrist (bends the palm toward the forearm)
Abduction of the wrist (radial deviation; tilts the hand toward the thumb side)
Assists weakly with forearm pronation
structures.locate: Rest your forearm palm-up on a table. Make a fist and bend your wrist toward you against light resistance: the most prominent tendon standing up in the middle of your wrist is palmaris longus, and the cord just to its thumb side is the flexor carpi radialis tendon. Trace that cord up toward the inner side of your elbow to feel the muscle belly.
structures.palpation: With the forearm supinated (palm up), resist wrist flexion and radial deviation; palpate the taut tendon at the front of the wrist on the thumb side of palmaris longus, and follow it proximally to the muscle belly in the upper-medial forearm.
commonProblems: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) from overload of the common flexor origin
Wrist flexor tendinopathy or strain from repetitive gripping and flexion
FCR tendinitis near its insertion, sometimes with trapezium/scaphoid arthritis

structures.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus muscle
structures.plainName: the long wrist-straightening muscle on the thumb side of your forearm — it cocks your wrist backward and tilts the hand toward the thumb
aka: Long radial extensor of the wrist

origin.text: The lower part of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus (the bony crest running up from the outer elbow), with a contribution from the lateral intermuscular septum of the arm.
origin.attachTo: humerus (lateral supracondylar ridge, below the origin of brachioradialis)

insertion.text: The tendon runs down the thumb side of the forearm and attaches to the back of the base of the second metacarpal bone (the hand bone leading to the index finger).
insertion.attachTo: posterior (dorsal) surface of the base of the second metacarpal

actions: wrist extension (cocking the back of the hand upward)
radial deviation of the wrist / abduction of the hand (tilting the hand toward the thumb side)
weakly assists elbow flexion
structures.locate: Rest your forearm palm-down on a table with the hand relaxed off the edge. With your other hand, feel the top of the forearm just below and beyond the bony bump on the outer (thumb-side) elbow. Now lift the back of your hand up toward the ceiling as if revving a motorbike throttle — the firm ridge of muscle that springs up there, running down toward the base of your index finger, is the extensor carpi radialis longus.
structures.palpation: With the forearm pronated and supported, palpate the upper posterolateral forearm just distal to the lateral epicondyle, deep to brachioradialis. Ask the patient to extend the wrist with slight radial deviation against resistance; the contracting muscle belly and its tendon (traceable toward the base of the second metacarpal) rise under the fingers.
commonProblems: lateral-epicondylitis-tennis-elbow
wrist-extensor-strain
radial-tunnel-syndrome

structures.name: Sternocleidomastoid muscle
structures.plainName: The rope-like muscle on the side of your neck

origin.text: Two heads: the sternal head from the front (manubrium) of the breastbone, and the clavicular head from the inner portion of the collarbone.
origin.attachTo: Manubrium of sternum and medial third of clavicle

insertion.text: The two heads join and attach to the bony bump behind the ear (mastoid process) and the ridge along the back of the skull (superior nuchal line).
insertion.attachTo: Mastoid process of the temporal bone and lateral half of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone

actions: Turns the head to the opposite side (one side contracting alone)
Tilts the head toward the same shoulder (one side contracting alone)
Bends the neck forward, bringing chin toward chest (both sides together); note that acting on a rigid neck it can instead extend the head at the top joints
Assists breathing in by lifting the breastbone and collarbone during hard inhalation

innervation.nerve: Accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) for motor supply; cervical plexus for sensory/proprioception

structures.locate: Turn your head to the left and look slightly up: a firm, rope-like band pops out on the RIGHT side of your neck, running from behind your right ear down to the notch at the top of your breastbone. Pinch it gently between finger and thumb. Turn the other way to feel it on the left.
structures.palpation: With the head rotated to the opposite side, grasp the prominent cord running from behind the ear to the sternoclavicular joint; roll it between fingers along its length. The sternal (tendinous) head is most distinct near its lower attachment at the top of the breastbone.
commonProblems: Torticollis (wry neck) - sustained spasm holding the head tilted and rotated
Congenital muscular torticollis in infants from a tight or fibrotic SCM
Trigger points referring pain to the head, face, ear, or behind the eye
Whiplash strain from sudden neck acceleration

structures.name: Adductor magnus muscle
structures.plainName: Great inner-thigh muscle

origin.text: Adductor part: the front branches of the pubic bone (inferior pubic ramus) and the branch of the sitting bone (ischial ramus). Hamstring part: the sitting bone itself (ischial tuberosity).

insertion.text: Adductor part: down the rough vertical ridge on the back of the thigh bone (linea aspera). Hamstring part: the adductor tubercle just above the inner knee. (Sources differ on whether the medial supracondylar line belongs to the adductor part or the hamstring part.)

actions: Pulls the thigh inward toward the midline (hip adduction) - both parts
Bends the hip, drawing the thigh forward (hip flexion) - adductor part
Straightens the hip, drawing the thigh backward (hip extension) - hamstring part

innervation.nerve: Dual supply: posterior branch of the obturator nerve (adductor part) and the tibial part of the sciatic nerve (hamstring part)
innervation.roots: Obturator L2-L4; tibial part of sciatic L4

structures.locate: Sit down and find your inner thigh. Press your fingers into the soft muscle on the inside of your thigh, high up near the groin, then trace it downward along the inner thigh toward a bony bump just above the inside of your knee. This large sheet of muscle running that whole length is the adductor magnus. Squeeze your knees together against your own hands and you will feel it firm up along the inner thigh.
structures.palpation: With the hip slightly bent and turned out, press into the inner thigh while squeezing the knees together against resistance; the muscle tightens under your fingers along the inner thigh from groin to just above the inner knee.

structures.name: Splenius capitis muscle
structures.plainName: Neck strap muscle (skull attachment)

origin.text: Lower half of the nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of the C7 to T3 vertebrae

insertion.text: Mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral part of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone

actions: Bilaterally: extends the head and neck (tilts the head back)
Unilaterally: laterally flexes the head to the same side (ear toward shoulder)
Unilaterally: rotates the head to the same side (turns the face toward the working side)

innervation.nerve: Lateral branches of the posterior (dorsal) rami of the middle cervical spinal nerves

synergists: Sternocleidomastoid (same side, for rotation to that side)
commonProblems: Neck stiffness and pain from prolonged forward-head posture at a desk or phone
Tension headaches referred to the top of the head
Muscle strain or 'crick' after sleeping in an awkward position or sudden neck movement
structures.locate: Feel for the bony bump just behind your ear (the mastoid process). The splenius capitis runs diagonally from there down and inward to the base of your neck and upper back. To feel it work, place your fingertips on the back of your neck, then tip your head backward or turn your face toward that same hand against light resistance and you will feel the muscle tighten under your fingers.
structures.palpation: Palpate in the upper posterior neck. A small portion is accessible in the triangle bounded by the sternocleidomastoid in front, the upper trapezius behind, and the levator scapulae below; most of the muscle lies deep to the trapezius. Turning the head to the same side against resistance makes the accessible part firm and easier to feel.

structures.name: Scalene muscles
structures.plainName: Side-of-neck breathing muscles

origin.text: Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae (C2–C7). The anterior scalene arises from the anterior tubercles of C3–C6, the middle scalene from the posterior tubercles of the lower six cervical vertebrae (C2–C7), and the posterior scalene from the posterior tubercles of the lower cervical vertebrae (commonly given as C5–C7; some sources give C4–C6).

insertion.text: First and second ribs. The anterior scalene attaches to the scalene tubercle on the inner border of the first rib; the middle scalene to the superior surface of the first rib behind the subclavian groove; the posterior scalene to the second rib (external/outer surface).

actions: Elevate the first and second ribs during forceful inhalation (accessory muscles of inspiration)
Bend the neck sideways toward the same side (ipsilateral lateral flexion) when one side contracts
Assist bending the neck forward when both sides contract together
Help stabilise the cervical spine against side-to-side movement

innervation.nerve: Anterior rami of the cervical spinal nerves

structures.locate: Put two fingers flat on the side of your neck, just above the collarbone and a little behind the big rope-like muscle (sternocleidomastoid) that stands out when you turn your head. Take a short, sharp sniff through your nose: the small band of muscle that tightens under your fingertips is the scalenes.
structures.palpation: Sit upright and find the sternocleidomastoid by turning your head to the opposite side. Slide your fingers just behind and above the collarbone, into the soft hollow at the base of the neck, and press gently. A quick sniff makes the scalenes contract and firm up under your fingers. Palpate lightly only — the brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalenes here.
commonProblems: Tightness from chronic upper-chest (shallow) breathing, which overworks the scalenes as accessory breathing muscles
Neck and shoulder tension linked to poor posture or a forward head position
Thoracic outlet syndrome: tight scalenes can compress the brachial plexus nerves or subclavian artery, causing tingling, numbness, or coldness in the arm and hand
Referred aching into the shoulder, chest, or upper arm from trigger points
antagonists: Deep posterior neck extensors (splenius capitis and splenius cervicis)
